book.title: The Telegraph All New Toughie Crossword, book 1

clue.text: Figure of speech used about university company

indicators.note: about means wrapped around, so the figure of speech goes round the next piece

blocks.note: a trope is a figure of speech such as a metaphor
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A professor's pet metaphor gets repeated all round the campus firm.
explanation.walkthrough: TROPE goes round U to give TROUPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a touring band of performers, a theatrical company.

clue.text: Variety actors always given the same role

blocks.note: a type is a variety or kind
the cast is the group of actors in a production

explanation.surface: A variety show's performers keep playing the same parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety' suggests music-hall entertainment, but it just means a kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A typecast actor is repeatedly given the same kind of part, so is always given the same role.

clue.text: Dance in set and open out

indicators.note: out here means put out of place, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dancers in a set of a square dance move out and spread apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open out' looks like one phrase meaning expand; the fodder is the two words set and open, and out alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-step is a ballroom dance of the early 20th century done in quick walking steps.

clue.text: Act as a football selector — see this in celebration after goal?

definitions.text: see this in celebration after goal?

blocks.note: first reading: to ..., choosing a defender for the side

blocks.clueFragment: see this in celebration after goal?
blocks.note: second reading: a ride on someone's shoulders, as a scorer may get from teammates

explanation.walkthrough: Read as three words, the answer is what a selector does: pick a back, a defensive player. Read as one word, it is a piggyback ride.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickaback is an older form of piggyback, carrying someone on your back, as players do with a goalscorer.

clue.text: Delightful cleaner assigned to LibDem politician

blocks.note: a char, or charlady, is a cleaning woman
Ming was the nickname of Sir Menzies Campbell, Liberal Democrat leader

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady is sent to work for a Liberal Democrat, and it is all very pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Liberal Democrats are a British party; their leader in 2006-07, Menzies Campbell, was universally called Ming.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming is an everyday synonym for delightful or very pleasing.

clue.text: Claudio was such a fan

blocks.note: surface reading: an Italian named Claudio was an ardent admirer of someone
setter's reading: Claudio in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing loves the heroine named Hero

explanation.walkthrough: Claudio's beloved in Much Ado About Nothing is called Hero, so his adoration makes him literally a worshipper of Hero.
explanation.definitionFit: A hero-worshipper is an excessive admirer, and Shakespeare's Claudio is devoted to a woman named Hero.

clue.text: Famous musician left after party

indicators.note: after places the single letter behind the party word rather than in front

blocks.note: a rave is a big dance party
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A celebrated musician walked out after the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as departed, but it is just the letter L.
explanation.definitionFit: Maurice Ravel was the French composer of Boléro, a famous musician.

clue.text: No paint for painting — artist in fix

indicators.note: no ... for means the named word is dropped from the next word, leaving the rest

blocks.note: the word taken as written before the cut
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword's usual artist
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painter has run out of paint for a canvas and is in a fix.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove PAINT from PAINTING to leave ING, then add RA and IN. 'In fix' looks like a phrase meaning in trouble, but fix is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingrain is to fix something deeply and firmly, as a habit or a dye in fabric.

clue.text: Litre- someone on errand collects it for player

indicators.note: collecting something means gathering it in, so the errand-runner takes the first piece inside

blocks.note: a gofer runs errands, going for things
L is the symbol for litre

explanation.surface: A runner sent for a litre of something brings it back for a sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash after 'Litre' splits it off as the piece to be collected; 'it' simply points back to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer is someone who plays golf, so a player of a sport.

clue.text: Legal instruction for mum

blocks.note: surface reading: a lawyer's advice or a court order concerning someone's mother
setter's reading: mum means keeping quiet, so this is a court's order to be quiet

explanation.walkthrough: Mum reads as mother, but keeping mum means staying silent; the instruction is the one a court usher or judge calls out.
explanation.definitionFit: The call for silence in court is a judicial instruction that everyone stay quiet, which is to keep mum.

clue.text: More self-righteous support stifles influence

indicators.note: to stifle is to smother, so one piece closes over and encloses the other

blocks.note: a pier is a pillar that supports a bridge or arch
one's reach is one's range of influence

explanation.surface: A backer who smothers someone's influence sounds sanctimonious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' reads as backing a person, but it is a structural pillar here.
explanation.definitionFit: Preachy means moralising and sanctimonious, so its comparative describes someone even more self-righteous.

clue.text: Watch poet run out

indicators.note: out means removed, so the letter for the following word is taken away

blocks.note: Virgil was the Roman poet of the Aeneid
R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Keep an eye on the poet as he is dismissed in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run out' looks like cricket; here run is R and out removes it from VIRGIL, leaving VIGIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A vigil is a period of keeping awake on guard, which is a watch in the noun sense.

clue.text: Too much to get into compartment in small dwelling

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a cage is an enclosed compartment, as for a lift
OTT is short for over the top, meaning excessive

explanation.surface: There is far too much to fit into the cupboard space of a tiny home.
explanation.walkthrough: Over the top is everyday British shorthand for excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A cottage is a small house, typically in the country, so it is a small dwelling.

clue.text: Scottish patriot, the top player at Eton?

blocks.note: the Eton wall game is a football game unique to Eton College
an ace is an expert, the best player

explanation.surface: A Scottish hero is hailed as the best sportsman at a famous English school.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is an English public school famous for its wall game, so the ace at Eton is a WALL ACE; WALLACE is William Wallace, the 13th-century Scottish leader.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wallace led Scottish resistance to Edward I and is Scotland's archetypal patriot.

clue.text: Barriers a pet's destroyed

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken up, so these letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An animal has wrecked the fences.
explanation.walkthrough: Septa is the plural of septum, the anatomical word for a dividing wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Septa are partitions separating cavities, as between the nostrils or heart chambers, so they are barriers.

clue.text: Woman in vehicle taking old route

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
O is the abbreviation for old
a line is a route, as a railway or bus line

explanation.surface: A woman drives along a road that has been used for centuries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' and 'taking' only join the pieces; the woman's name comes from CAR, O and LINE in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: Caroline is a female first name, and crosswords often define names simply as woman or girl.

clue.text: Cheese — food served up beset by fruit, right?

indicators.note: in a down answer up means bottom to top, so the food is written backwards
beset means surrounded, so the fruit closes round the food

blocks.note: a lime is a citrus fruit
grub is informal for food
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A cheese course is brought up surrounded by fruit; is that correct?
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal happens first, then the fruit goes round it, then the single letter is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Limburger is a strong-smelling soft cheese from the Limburg region of Belgium and the Netherlands.

clue.text: Ruse — is learner involved to get evicted?

definitions.note: a verb meaning to force out; the clue's passive phrase is loose for it

indicators.note: involved means wrapped up inside, so these letters go within the ruse

blocks.note: a dodge is a trick or ruse
taken as written
L is for learner, from the L-plates of a learner driver

explanation.surface: A tenant wonders whether a trick involving a trainee will get them thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: D(ISL)ODGE. The definition reads loosely: to dislodge someone is to get them evicted.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislodge is to force someone or something out of position, as an eviction removes a tenant.

clue.text: Matey saying "I care nothing for Saul's dad!""

indicators.note: saying signals that the words are to be spoken, so the answer matches their sound

blocks.clueFragment: I care nothing for Saul's dad
blocks.note: 'Blow' is an exclamation of not caring; Kish was Saul's father in the Book of Samuel

explanation.surface: A friendly chap declares that he could not care less about King Saul's father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow him!' is British slang for dismissing someone; saying 'blow Kish' gives the sound of BLOKEISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Blokeish means like a typical bloke, hearty and pally, which is what matey describes.

clue.text: "Pond feature" woman acquired at front of residence

indicators.note: at the front places the woman ahead of the home rather than after it

blocks.note: Lily is a woman's name
pad is slang for a home or flat

explanation.surface: A woman has bought a house with a pond as its selling point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acquired' only joins the woman to the home; the quotation marks round the definition are the setter's flourish.
explanation.definitionFit: A lily pad is the large floating leaf of a water lily, a familiar sight on a pond.

clue.text: An African, I, a man heading west

indicators.note: in an across answer west is leftward, so the letters are written right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
Sam is a man's name

explanation.surface: A traveller in Africa describes himself as a man setting off westward.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows a stray bar where the pronoun I belongs. I, A and SAM run backwards to give MASAI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Masai are a pastoral people of Kenya and Tanzania, so a Masai is an African.

clue.text: A very little fly falls into tin

indicators.note: falling into something means dropping inside it, so the insect goes within the metal

blocks.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
a midge is a tiny fly

explanation.surface: A tiny insect tumbles into a can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A very little fly' wants to be one phrase; the definition stops at little, and fly is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A smidgen is a tiny amount, so 'a smidgen' stands for 'a very little', as in a very little sugar.

clue.text: Short comment seen in newspaper cutting

indicators.note: seen in says the letters can be spotted inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the run of letters from the end of the first word to the start of the second

explanation.surface: A brief remark appears in a clipping from the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: newsp-APER CU-tting.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperçu is a brief, pithy comment or insight, borrowed from French.

clue.text: European host, one coming in for verbal attack

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so one piece is placed inside the host word

blocks.note: a Pole is a person from Poland
MC, master of ceremonies, is a host
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A European presenter has someone arriving to deliver a tirade.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the one goes inside the host; the European stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemic is a strongly worded written or spoken attack on an opinion, so it is a verbal attack.

clue.text: Not old-fashioned boy according to a statistical measure

blocks.note: mod is short for modern
Al is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A trendy lad is described in terms of statistics.
explanation.walkthrough: MOD then AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Modal means relating to the mode, the statistical measure for the most frequent value in a set.

clue.text: Friend admitting common love, one of cats and dogs?

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the friend takes the following pieces inside

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
luv is the colloquial spelling of love as a form of address
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A friend lets in a common darling who is a pet owner of cats and dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: P(LUV I)AL. 'One of cats and dogs' wants to be a pet; the definition is 'of cats and dogs', from the phrase raining cats and dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pluvial means relating to rain, and heavy rain is said to come down as cats and dogs.

clue.text: Speedy incursion to capture president

indicators.note: capturing means seizing and holding, so the raid closes round the next piece

blocks.note: a raid is a sudden incursion
P is the abbreviation for president

explanation.surface: A lightning raid is launched to seize a head of state.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapid and speedy are straightforward synonyms meaning fast.

clue.text: Bad egg, duenna — so girl stays thus?

indicators.note: something bad has gone wrong, so these letters are spoilt into a different order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wicked chaperone keeps her charge from any suitor.
explanation.walkthrough: A duenna is an older woman chaperoning a girl in Spain or Portugal; a strict one keeps her charge from being promised in marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Unengaged means not betrothed, the state a closely chaperoned girl is kept in.

clue.text: Surge a bit less than extreme and coming after expected time

indicators.note: a bit less than means slightly short, so the following word loses its final letter

blocks.note: undue means excessive, beyond what is warranted
late means arriving after the expected time

explanation.surface: A wave of feeling, slightly short of extreme, arrives behind schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surge' looks like part of the wordplay's scene, but it is the definition: the sea surging is the sea rising and falling.
explanation.definitionFit: To undulate is to rise and fall in waves, which is what the sea does when it surges.

clue.text: Recoil in church, carrying something for the wedding

indicators.note: carrying means holding something inside, so the church wraps round the next piece

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
a ring is exchanged at a wedding

explanation.surface: Someone flinches in church while holding the wedding band.
explanation.walkthrough: CE, the Church of England, is the usual crossword church.
explanation.definitionFit: To cringe is to shrink back in fear or embarrassment, which is to recoil.
